question.text: If the boiling point of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>373</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math>, and  the boiling point of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></math> will be :

options.text: greater than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>300</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math> but less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>373</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math>

solution.text: At room temperature water is liquid and has boiling points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>373</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math> due to hydrogen bonding. Where as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></math> is gas and it has no hydrogen bonding. Hence boiling point of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></math> is less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>300</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math> [Boiling point of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>-</mo><mn>60</mn></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>]
